title: The wording points at expiry, not a bad password
explanation: `su - etl -c 'echo ok'` prints `Your account has expired; please contact your system administrator.` — a distinct message from a wrong-password prompt or a `nologin`-style lockout. That specific phrase means the account itself has an expiry date, checked separately from whatever the password field holds.

title: Read the aging fields directly rather than guessing
explanation: `sudo chage -l etl` lists every account-aging field at once, including `Account expires`. Here it shows a date back in 1970 — long past — confirming this is a hard expiry, not a max-password-age or inactivity setting.

title: Expiry and a password lock are enforced differently, and that difference matters here
explanation: `passwd -l` (a password lock) blocks password-based logins, but root invoking `su` doesn't need to supply a password, so it sails right past that kind of lock. Account expiry (`chage -E`) is a separate check that fires regardless of who's asking — including root — which is exactly why `su - etl` still fails even run by trainee with full sudo.

title: Clear the expiry, don't just delete and recreate the account
explanation: `sudo chage -E -1 etl` sets the expiry to `-1` (never expires), correcting the one field that's actually blocking things without touching the account's UID, home directory, or anything else it owns.

title: Verify the field, then the actual behavior
explanation: `sudo chage -l etl` should now read `Account expires: never`, and re-running the exact command from step 1 confirms the account is genuinely usable again — not just that a config value changed on paper.
